docTitle: 8 edge cases that break real apps (with the real stories)

slides.title: 8 edge cases that *break real apps*
slides.sub: Each one is a real story, from a woman named Null to the leap day that took down part of Azure.

slides.title: We test the form the way we hope people will use it
slides.body: Real users double-click, open different tabs and lose their network halfway. I promise you, someone is going to report the edge case you never thought of.

slides.title: One double click, two orders
slides.body: Disabling the button stops the double click. An idempotency key (a unique ID per request) also stops retries and second tabs.

slides.title: 1 left, *2 sold*
slides.code: UPDATE products SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE id = 42 AND stock > 0 -- 0 rows updated = sold out
slides.body: If two requests arrive at the same time, only one of them can take the last item. The other one gets zero rows updated. In 2015 a researcher used this kind of bug to turn $15 of Starbucks gift cards into $20.

slides.title: The name O'Brien can break your query

fields.label: Surname
fields.msg: The apostrophe breaks the SQL query

slides.body: The apostrophe is the character that starts and ends text in SQL. If your code glues the name straight into the query, it breaks. The BBC also wrote about Jennifer Null, whose surname gets read as empty.

slides.title: A licence plate that said NULL got *$12,000 in fines*
slides.body: Security researcher Joseph Tartaro told the story at DEF CON in 2019. Tickets with no plate on them ended up with his name, because the system read NULL as a plate.

slides.title: 29 February 2012 + 1 year = a date that doesn't exist
slides.body: Microsoft's own summary says the code was “simply taking the current date and adding one to its year”. Creating the certificate failed, and part of Azure went down with it.

slides.title: In Tallinn, 3:30 a.m. happened twice
slides.body: In Estonia where I live, the clock changes twice a year. A job scheduled for 3:30 skips one day and runs twice on another.

slides.title: Adébáyọ̀ is 7 letters and 13 bytes
slides.body: In PHP, strlen counts bytes and mb_strlen counts characters. Normalise the text before you save it, too.

slides.title: Whatever your API does, someone *depends on it*
slides.quote: With a sufficient number of users of an API, it does not matter what you promise in the contract: all observable behaviors of your system will be depended on by somebody.
slides.by: Hyrum's law, named after Hyrum Wright
slides.body: If your API always returned a list in the same order, someone's code now depends on that order, even though you never promised it.

slides.title: Which edge case would you add?
slides.body: You can't predict every single one. If you wait till you can, you probably wouldn't ship anything.
